title: #72 After a Cold Call Write the Student's Answer on the Board
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton extends an earlier point about giving students time to think after a peer's answer, arguing that teachers routinely undercut that thinking time by reacting to a Cold Call answer immediately -- either confirming or rejecting it or redirecting to another student -- before anyone has had a real chance to process it. His proposed intervention is to write the answer on the board immediately after it's given, before making any evaluative move: in his example, a student answers that 7% as a decimal is 0.7, and rather than responding right away, the teacher first writes "0.7" large enough for the whole class to see. He argues the few seconds this buys are valuable thinking time for both students and teacher, and that a written answer is more durable than a spoken one, giving students a stable reference point for whatever discussion follows. He explicitly ties the benefit to the transient information effect, framing the written answer as protection against the fact that spoken information disappears the moment it's said.
points: Teachers habitually respond to a Cold Call answer immediately, which forecloses the thinking time the response was meant to trigger for the rest of the class.
The intervention is a small procedural pause, not a bigger pedagogical shift: write the answer on the board before making any evaluative or follow-up move.

Barton explicitly grounds the technique in the transient information effect -- a spoken answer vanishes the instant it's said, while a written one remains available as a stable reference point for the discussion that follows.

The three-second delay serves two audiences at once: it gives students time to process the answer and gives the teacher a brief buffer to decide their own next move deliberately rather than reflexively.
quotes: In newsletter #17, I wrote about giving students enough time to think after hearing another student’s answer.
All too often, teachers respond immediately to a student’s answer, either saying it is correct or not, or asking another student what they think of the answer.
A way to combat this urge is to write students’ answers on the board after they have said them.

Instead of making your next move (for example, telling Molly she is incorrect, asking another student what they think, or instigating a Turn and Talk), you first write Molly’s answer on the board, nice and big so everyone can see.
The three seconds this takes are vital to give your students and yourself time to process Molly’s answer.
Hence, it acts as a frame of reference for whatever move you make next, avoiding falling victim to the transient information effect.
